questions.stem: Which of the following organisms is a common cause of surgical site infection after abdominal surgery?
questions.explanation: Staphylococcus aureus is the most frequent pathogen in post‑operative wound infections. Streptococcus pyogenes and Candida can cause infections but less common; Pseudomonas is usually associated with contaminated environments.

questions.stem: A 45‑year‑old patient develops a fever and a purulent discharge from a laparotomy wound 5 days post‑operation. Gram‑positive cocci in clusters are isolated. What is the most likely organism?
questions.explanation: Staphylococcus aureus is the classic cause of purulent wound infection. Staphylococcus epidermidis is less virulent; Streptococcus agalactiae and Enterococcus are less common in this setting.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the most effective pre‑operative skin antiseptic to reduce surgical site infections?
questions.explanation: Chlorhexidine with alcohol provides superior skin decolonisation and lower SSI rates compared with povidone‑iodine or saline. Sodium hypochlorite is not used for skin prep.

questions.stem: A patient with a known allergy to penicillin is undergoing a clean‑contaminated surgery. Which antibiotic is the best choice for prophylaxis?
questions.explanation: Clindamycin is the preferred alternative for patients allergic to beta‑lactams. Gentamicin and metronidazole lack broad coverage; vancomycin is reserved for MRSA.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a characteristic of gram‑negative rods that are commonly implicated in intra‑abdominal infections?
options: They possess a thick peptidoglycan layer
They have an outer membrane containing lipopolysaccharide
questions.explanation: Gram‑negative rods have an outer membrane with LPS, contributing to endotoxin release. Thick peptidoglycan is a gram‑positive feature; catalase positivity is not specific; they are not cocci.

questions.stem: Which of the following organisms is most likely to cause a postoperative intra‑abdominal abscess in a patient who had a perforated diverticulitis?
questions.explanation: E. coli is the predominant enteric pathogen in diverticulitis‑related abscesses. Staph aureus is less common; C. difficile causes colitis; Pseudomonas is uncommon in this context.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a key feature of the innate immune response to bacterial infection?
options: Release of pro‑inflammatory cytokines by macrophages
questions.explanation: Macrophages release cytokines (IL‑1, TNF‑α) as part of innate immunity. IgM and complement fixation are adaptive responses; T‑cell receptors are part of adaptive immunity.

questions.stem: A patient with a history of chronic steroid use develops a fever and a purulent drainage from a surgical incision. Which organism is most likely responsible?
questions.explanation: Staphylococcus aureus is the most common pathogen in surgical site infections, especially in immunosuppressed patients. The others are less likely causes of acute wound infection.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the most common cause of postoperative sepsis in patients undergoing colorectal surgery?
questions.explanation: E. coli, a gut flora organism, is the leading cause of postoperative sepsis after colorectal procedures. Enterococcus and Staph epidermidis are less common; Pseudomonas is rare.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a characteristic of a gram‑positive cocci that is resistant to vancomycin?
options: It has a thick peptidoglycan layer
It has a modified D‑alanine residue in the cell wall
questions.explanation: Vancomycin resistance in gram‑positive cocci (e.g., MRSA) is due to altered D‑alanine residues, reducing drug binding. Thick peptidoglycan and beta‑lactamase are unrelated; teichoic acids are present.

questions.stem: A 60‑year‑old man with diabetes develops a deep surgical wound infection. Which of the following organisms is most likely to be isolated?
questions.explanation: Staphylococcus aureus is the most common pathogen in diabetic wound infections. Streptococcus pyogenes and Clostridium perfringens are less frequent; Pseudomonas is uncommon in clean wounds.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a typical feature of a fungal infection of a surgical wound?
options: High neutrophil count in wound exudate
Presence of hyphae on Gram stain
questions.explanation: Fungal infections show hyphae or spores on special stains; they do not produce pus or high neutrophils, and eosinophilia is not a typical feature.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate prophylactic antibiotic for a patient undergoing a clean‑contaminated laparoscopic cholecystectomy?
questions.explanation: Cefazolin covers skin flora and is standard for clean‑contaminated abdominal procedures. Ampicillin is less effective; metronidazole covers anaerobes but not skin flora; vancomycin is reserved for MRSA.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a key component of the adaptive immune response that provides long‑term protection against bacterial pathogens?
questions.explanation: Memory B cells persist after infection and enable rapid antibody production upon re‑exposure. Complement and phagocytosis are innate; pattern‑recognition receptors are part of innate immunity.

questions.stem: A 45‑year‑old man presents with a purulent wound after a dog bite. Which organism is most likely responsible for the infection?
questions.explanation: Pasteurella multocida is the classic pathogen in animal bite wounds, especially from cats and dogs. Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus pyogenes are common skin flora, while Pseudomonas is more associated with water exposure.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the most common cause of postoperative surgical site infection in clean‑contaminated abdominal procedures?
questions.explanation: E. coli, part of the normal gut flora, is the predominant organism in clean‑contaminated abdominal surgeries. Enterococcus and Staphylococcus epidermidis are less common, and Streptococcus pneumoniae is not a typical abdominal pathogen.

questions.stem: A patient with a history of penicillin allergy develops a severe skin rash after receiving amoxicillin. Which immune mechanism is most likely responsible?
questions.explanation: Amoxicillin‑induced rash is a classic IgE‑mediated Type I hypersensitivity reaction. Type II involves antibody‑mediated cytotoxicity, Type III immune complex deposition, and Type IV delayed‑type T‑cell reaction.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the best initial step in managing a patient with suspected septic arthritis of the knee?
options: Obtain arthrocentesis for synovial fluid analysis
Order an MRI of the knee
questions.explanation: Synovial fluid analysis is essential to confirm infection and guide therapy. Empiric antibiotics and imaging are secondary steps.

questions.stem: In a patient with a central venous catheter, the most common pathogen causing catheter‑related bloodstream infection is:
questions.explanation: Staphylococcus epidermidis, a skin commensal, is the leading cause of catheter‑related bloodstream infections. Candida and Gram‑negative rods are less common.

questions.stem: A 60‑year‑old diabetic patient develops a foot ulcer that has become necrotic. Which organism is most likely responsible for the polymicrobial infection?
questions.explanation: Diabetic foot ulcers are typically polymicrobial, involving both anaerobes and aerobes. Single organisms are less likely to explain the extensive necrosis.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a characteristic feature of a Gram‑positive cocci that is catalase negative?
questions.explanation: Streptococcus species are catalase negative; Staphylococcus species are catalase positive. Enterococcus is also catalase negative but is a Gram‑positive coccus in chains, not the typical answer.

questions.stem: The presence of which virulence factor is most important in the pathogenesis of Clostridium difficile colitis?
questions.explanation: Both exotoxins A and B are essential for the cytotoxic effect in C. difficile infection. Spore formation aids transmission but is not the key virulence factor.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate empiric antibiotic regimen for a patient with a suspected necrotizing fasciitis?
questions.explanation: Piperacillin‑tazobactam covers Gram‑positive, Gram‑negative, and anaerobes, and clindamycin suppresses toxin production. The other regimens lack adequate coverage.

questions.stem: A patient undergoing elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy develops a postoperative fever and leukocytosis. The most likely source of infection is:
questions.explanation: Post‑operative fever after laparoscopic cholecystectomy is most often due to a superficial wound infection. Bile leak and pneumonia are less common, and UTI is unlikely without instrumentation.

questions.stem: Which of the following organisms is most resistant to penicillin due to the production of beta‑lactamase?
questions.explanation: Methicillin‑resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) produces beta‑lactamase and is resistant to penicillin. The other organisms are generally susceptible.

questions.stem: A 30‑year‑old woman presents with a sore throat, fever, and a rash on the palms and soles. Which pathogen is most likely responsible?
questions.explanation: Streptococcus pyogenes causes scarlet fever, characterized by fever, sore throat, and a sandpaper rash on palms and soles. The other options do not produce this rash pattern.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the most common cause of fungal infection in a patient with a long‑term central venous catheter?
questions.explanation: Candida albicans is the predominant fungal pathogen in catheter‑related bloodstream infections. The others are less common.

questions.stem: A patient with a history of chronic alcoholism presents with a sudden onset of severe abdominal pain and a high white cell count. Which organism is most likely responsible for the acute pancreatitis?
questions.explanation: Clostridium perfringens can cause gas gangrene and is a known cause of acute pancreatitis in alcoholics. The other organisms are not typical culprits.

questions.stem: A 45‑year‑old man presents with a purulent wound after a dog bite. Gram staining shows Gram‑positive cocci in chains. Which organism is most likely responsible?
questions.explanation: Staphylococcus aureus is the commonest cause of dog‑bite infections and appears as Gram‑positive cocci in clusters, not chains. The other streptococci are less common in such wounds.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the most specific test for diagnosing a fungal infection of the skin?
questions.explanation: KOH preparation dissolves keratin and reveals fungal hyphae or spores directly from skin scrapings, making it the most specific bedside test for dermatophytes. The other stains are for bacteria or acid‑fast organisms.

questions.stem: A patient undergoing elective laparotomy receives a prophylactic dose of cefazolin. Which of the following is the best explanation for its effectiveness?
options: It blocks bacterial cell wall synthesis
questions.explanation: Cefazolin is a first‑generation cephalosporin that inhibits transpeptidase, blocking peptidoglycan cross‑linking and thus cell wall synthesis. The other mechanisms describe other antibiotic classes.

questions.stem: A 30‑year‑old woman has a chronic sinus infection. Cultures grow a gram‑negative rod that is oxidase positive and grows well on chocolate agar but not on MacConkey agar. Which organism is most likely?
questions.explanation: Haemophilus influenzae is a small, oxidase‑positive, fastidious gram‑negative rod that requires factors X and V and grows on chocolate agar but not on MacConkey. The others are non‑fastidious and grow on MacConkey.

questions.stem: Which of the following immunoglobulin subclasses is primarily responsible for complement activation in the classical pathway?
questions.explanation: IgG3 has the highest capacity to activate complement via the classical pathway due to its long hinge region. IgG1 can also activate but less efficiently; IgG2 and IgG4 are poor activators.

questions.stem: A patient with a history of recurrent urinary tract infections is found to have a urinary catheter. Which organism is most likely to form a biofilm on the catheter surface?
questions.explanation: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is notorious for forming robust biofilms on indwelling devices. Staphylococcus epidermidis also forms biofilms but is more common on prosthetic joints; the others are less biofilm‑prone.

questions.stem: A 60‑year‑old man develops a sudden, painless loss of vision in one eye. Fundoscopy shows a pale retina with a cherry‑red spot. Which pathogen is most commonly associated with this presentation?
questions.explanation: Optic neuropathy with a cherry‑red spot is classic for neurosyphilis (Treponema pallidum). The other organisms are not associated with this ocular finding.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the most reliable method for detecting methicillin resistance in Staphylococcus aureus?
questions.explanation: PCR for the mecA gene directly identifies the genetic determinant of methicillin resistance. Disk diffusion with oxacillin is less sensitive; Etest for vancomycin and MIC for penicillin do not detect methicillin resistance.

questions.stem: A patient with a severe burn injury develops a rapidly spreading infection. Gram staining shows gram‑negative rods with a characteristic “safety‑pin” appearance. Which organism is most likely?
questions.explanation: Pseudomonas aeruginosa produces a safety‑pin appearance on Gram stain due to its polar flagella and is a common burn wound pathogen. The other organisms do not show this morphology.

questions.stem: A 25‑year‑old woman presents with a painful, erythematous ulcer on the vulva. Histology shows neutrophilic microabscesses in the dermis. Which organism is most likely?
questions.explanation: Streptococcus pyogenes causes erythema multiforme‑like lesions with neutrophilic microabscesses. Candida causes superficial yeast infection; Trichophyton causes tinea; Haemophilus ducreyi causes chancroid with a different histology.

questions.stem: Which cytokine is most directly involved in the recruitment of neutrophils to sites of bacterial infection?
questions.explanation: Interleukin‑8 (IL‑8) is a chemokine that specifically attracts neutrophils. IL‑2 and IFN‑γ are T‑cell activators; TNF‑α is a general pro‑inflammatory cytokine.

questions.stem: A 70‑year‑old man with a history of chronic liver disease develops a sudden, severe abdominal pain and a palpable mass. Imaging shows a large, irregular mass with central necrosis. Which organism is most likely responsible for this infection?
questions.explanation: Clostridium perfringens causes gas gangrene with rapid necrosis and a characteristic mass; the other organisms are less likely to produce such an acute, necrotic presentation.
